questions.question: Does behavioural profiling catch misuse of an identity's own access?
questions.answer: Yes. The frozen model reached 16 of 18 insiders it had never seen on a sealed six-month holdout, with one investigation a day.
questions.evidence: Strong: sealed holdout, scorers frozen before labels were read

questions.question: Can it start without labels?
questions.answer: Partly. A label-free rarity detector reaches about half of what the supervised model does; learning from analyst verdicts on its own cases closes most of the gap.
questions.evidence: Moderate: development folds, simulated analyst, two settings tried

questions.question: Does it catch a hijacked account in use?
questions.answer: No. In the takeover scenario it sees the attacker preparing under their own account, but no day on the hijacked account ever passed the gate. Profiling one identity at a time cannot link the victim's change to the attacker.
questions.evidence: Descriptive re-measurement of already reported results; small counts

bars.label: Attacker's own account · days over gate

questions.unit: labelled takeover days scoring over the gate (November and holdout)
questions.note: Takeover-aware population features did not change this (reports/BACKTEST-LEDGER.md). Of 29 detector variants in the methods study, only edge, edge_causal, gru_next reached a hijacked account at all, each in at most 1 incident-fold.

questions.question: Does the choice of detector matter?
questions.answer: Labels and a non-linear model matter most. The Random Forest and a neural network reach the most incidents; a sequence model ranks as well but reaches them later; a linear model and every label-free family land far below. Refining the implementations changed none of these comparisons.
questions.evidence: Exploratory: development folds only, paired bootstrap intervals
